cards.statement: A GET request has the same method semantics in HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3.
cards.explanation: HTTP versions change how messages travel, while the shared method semantics retain their meaning.

cards.statement: An HTTP/1.1 client derives a response's status meaning from its reason phrase.
cards.explanation: The numeric status code carries a response's status meaning. A reason phrase is recommended text that may be replaced or omitted.
cards.misconception: The reason phrase determines how a client interprets the response status.

cards.statement: In HTTP/1.1, a recipient treats the field names Content-Type and content-type as the same field.
cards.explanation: RFC 9110 defines field names as case-insensitive, so an HTTP/1.1 recipient matches Content-Type whatever its capitalization.

cards.statement: A recipient may combine repeated list-field lines into a comma-separated value in their received order.
cards.explanation: A recipient may combine list-field values with commas while preserving their received order; that order can affect interpretation.

cards.statement: A sender can use two Content-Type field lines to describe two possible media types for one message.
cards.explanation: Content-Type has single-value syntax. A sender must not repeat it to supply a list of alternative media types.
cards.misconception: Repeated field lines let a sender turn a single-valued field into a list.

source.title: RFC 9110 §5.3: Sender Restrictions on Repeated Fields

cards.statement: A server silently ignores request fields that exceed the size it is willing to process.
cards.explanation: A server must answer oversized request fields with an appropriate 4xx response when they exceed what it wishes to process.
cards.misconception: A server may discard oversized request fields and continue processing the request.

cards.statement: An intermediary may discard trailer fields while forwarding an HTTP message.
cards.explanation: Intermediaries can discard trailers in transit, so a server should keep information essential to the user agent out of them.

cards.statement: RFC 9110 lets a recipient assume http URIs whose hosts differ only in letter case identify the same resource.
cards.explanation: Scheme and host are case-insensitive in http and https URIs, and URIs that are equivalent after normalization can be assumed to identify the same resource.

cards.statement: A sender should put a username and password in an https target URI to supply credentials.
cards.explanation: User:password userinfo is deprecated. A sender must not generate userinfo in an http or https target URI within an HTTP message.
cards.misconception: Embedding user:password in a target URI is a recommended HTTP authentication mechanism.

cards.statement: A DELETE whose repeat gets 404 after a first 204 counts as non-idempotent under RFC 9110.
cards.explanation: DELETE stays idempotent even when a repeated request gets a different response, such as 404 after 204. Idempotence concerns the intended effect on the server, not identical status codes.
cards.misconception: A method is idempotent only if repeating it returns the same status code.

cards.statement: A proxy may retry a non-idempotent request automatically after the connection fails.
cards.explanation: A proxy must not automatically retry a non-idempotent request, including after a connection failure.
cards.misconception: A connection failure permits a proxy to replay a non-idempotent request automatically.

cards.statement: A server answering HEAD should send the header fields it would send for GET.
cards.explanation: A HEAD response should match GET's header fields. A server may omit fields whose values are determined only while generating content.

cards.statement: An origin server sends 201 when a successful PUT creates the target resource's first representation.
cards.explanation: A successful PUT that creates the target resource's first representation requires a 201 response.

cards.statement: A cache uses explicit freshness alone to establish the cacheability of a POST response.
cards.explanation: A cacheable POST response needs explicit freshness and Content-Location equal to the POST's target URI.
cards.misconception: Explicit freshness is sufficient to make a POST response cacheable.

cards.statement: A server sends an ETag in a successful PUT response even after transforming the submitted content.
cards.explanation: A successful PUT response must omit validators if the server transformed the submitted content before saving it.
cards.misconception: A server may return a validator for transformed content in a successful PUT response.

cards.statement: An origin server includes Allow in a 405 response to list the resource's supported methods.
cards.explanation: A 405 response must include Allow. The field identifies the methods the target resource currently supports.

cards.statement: PATCH has idempotent method semantics for a resource's partial updates.
cards.explanation: PATCH is not idempotent by definition. An individual patch can still be designed so repetition has the same intended effect.
cards.misconception: Partial updates make PATCH inherently idempotent.

cards.statement: QUERY is a safe method even though its request content carries the query.
cards.explanation: QUERY defines safe retrieval using request content to express the query; the client does not request a state change to the target resource.

cards.statement: A client uses an asterisk target in OPTIONS to ask about the server's general communication options.
cards.explanation: OPTIONS with an asterisk target concerns the server in general, rather than a particular target resource.

cards.statement: A client interprets an unrecognized 4xx status code as 400.
cards.explanation: A client must treat an unfamiliar status code as the x00 code of its class; an unfamiliar 4xx therefore has 400 semantics.

cards.statement: A server's 202 response confirms that processing the requested action succeeds.
cards.explanation: 202 means the server accepted the request for processing. Processing remains incomplete and the eventual outcome is uncertain.
cards.misconception: Acceptance for processing guarantees successful completion.

cards.statement: A server includes updated form content in a 205 Reset Content response.
cards.explanation: A server must not generate content in a 205 response. The response asks the user agent to reset the view used to submit the request.
cards.misconception: 205 supplies replacement content for the form the user agent should reset.

cards.statement: An origin server sending 401 Unauthorized includes a WWW-Authenticate field in that response.
cards.explanation: A server generating 401 must include a WWW-Authenticate challenge applicable to the target resource.

cards.statement: A server's 404 response tells the client that the resource's absence is permanent.
cards.explanation: 404 leaves the duration of the resource's absence unspecified; it does not establish that the absence is permanent.
cards.misconception: 404 establishes that a resource is permanently absent.

cards.statement: A server uses 415 for unsupported formats it discovers by inspecting request content.
cards.explanation: A server can discover an unsupported format by examining the request data itself, rather than relying on its declared Content-Type.

cards.statement: A server can use 422 Unprocessable Content for a request whose content has malformed syntax.
cards.explanation: 422 concerns content with valid syntax and an understood content type whose instructions the server cannot process.
cards.misconception: 422 reports malformed content syntax rather than unprocessable instructions.

cards.statement: A server's 429 response may include Retry-After to suggest a delay before another request.
cards.explanation: A 429 response may include Retry-After to advise when the client should try again; the field is optional.

cards.statement: A gateway uses 502 Bad Gateway when an upstream server fails to answer within the allotted time.
cards.explanation: An upstream timeout calls for 504 Gateway Timeout. A 502 reports an invalid response from an upstream server.
cards.misconception: 502 represents an upstream timeout rather than an invalid upstream response.

cards.statement: A user agent preserves the request method when it automatically follows a 307 redirect.
cards.explanation: A user agent must retain the request method when automatically following a 307 response.

cards.statement: A server's 303 response presents Location as an equivalent URI for the target resource.
cards.explanation: A 303 points to a resource supplying an indirect response. Its Location URI is not considered equivalent to the original target URI.
cards.misconception: 303 declares the redirect destination equivalent to the original target URI.

cards.statement: A cache classifies 308 Permanent Redirect as heuristically cacheable.
cards.explanation: 308 is heuristically cacheable, subject to the request method and explicit cache controls.

cards.statement: A user agent resolves a relative Location value against the request's target URI.
cards.explanation: The user agent resolves a relative redirect Location against the request's target URI to obtain the destination.

cards.statement: A user agent discards the old fragment when Location omits a fragment in a redirect.
cards.explanation: A redirect Location with no fragment inherits the fragment, if any, of the original URI reference used to generate the target URI.
cards.misconception: Omitting a fragment from Location clears the original URI reference's fragment.

cards.statement: A server's 300 response offers representations for the user agent to choose between.
cards.explanation: 300 offers alternatives so the user agent or user can select a preferred representation.

cards.statement: With fetch(), a browser preserves Authorization when a redirect reaches another origin.
cards.explanation: HTTP-redirect fetch removes Authorization once the redirect reaches an origin different from the request's current origin.
cards.misconception: Authorization follows a fetch() redirect across origins unchanged.

cards.statement: With fetch(), a browser changes a POST request to GET when following a 302 redirect.
cards.explanation: For a 302 response to POST, HTTP-redirect fetch changes the method to GET.

cards.statement: With fetch(), a browser keeps request-body headers when a redirect changes the method to GET.
cards.explanation: When HTTP-redirect fetch changes a method to GET, it deletes request-body headers such as Content-Type.
cards.misconception: Request-body metadata survives a redirect that rewrites the method to GET.

cards.statement: A user agent changes QUERY to GET when it follows a 301 redirect.
cards.explanation: QUERY retains its method on a 301 redirect. The historical POST-to-GET exception does not apply to QUERY.
cards.misconception: 301 applies the historical POST method-rewriting exception to QUERY.

cards.statement: A recipient matches media type names such as Text/HTML and text/html case-sensitively.
cards.explanation: Media type names are case-insensitive: changing the case of the type or subtype leaves the media type unchanged.
cards.misconception: Media type names are case-sensitive, so Text/HTML and text/html differ.

cards.statement: A recipient may assume application/octet-stream when a sender omits Content-Type.
cards.explanation: RFC 9110 permits this fallback when Content-Type is absent; it also permits the recipient to examine the data to determine its type.

cards.statement: A server uses Content-Language to list the languages that appear anywhere in the content.
cards.explanation: Content-Language describes the representation's intended audience. It need not list every language that appears in the content.
cards.misconception: Content-Language inventories the languages used in the content.

cards.statement: A user agent follows a response's Content-Location field by requesting that URI.
cards.explanation: Content-Location identifies a resource corresponding to the enclosed representation. The field is metadata, rather than a redirect instruction.
cards.misconception: Content-Location works like Location and makes the user agent fetch another URI.

cards.statement: An origin server uses the most specific matching Accept range to determine a representation's quality.
cards.explanation: A representation's quality comes from its most specific matching Accept range. A broad wildcard does not override that range's quality.

cards.statement: A client uses a zero quality value in Accept to mark a media range as unacceptable.
cards.explanation: A quality value of zero excludes the associated media range from the client's stated acceptable choices.

cards.statement: Under RFC 9110, a request that omits Accept-Language signals a preference for English.
cards.explanation: RFC 9110 says a request lacking a content negotiation field, such as Accept-Language, implies that the sender has no preference on that dimension.
cards.misconception: A request without Accept-Language means the client prefers English.

cards.statement: A server may disregard Accept preferences when its available representations fail to satisfy them.
cards.explanation: RFC 9110 allows the server to disregard unsatisfied negotiation preferences instead of returning 406. The result might be unusable to the client.

cards.statement: A client can rely on Accept-Language order as a standardized priority ranking for languages with equal quality values.
cards.explanation: Equal-quality language tags have no reliably interoperable order-based priority. Distinct quality values communicate differing priorities.
cards.misconception: The order of equal-quality language tags reliably establishes their priority.

cards.statement: A server's response Accept field advertises preferred media types for later requests to that resource.
cards.explanation: Accept in a response guides the content of a subsequent request to the same resource, using the server's media type preferences.

cards.statement: A user agent interprets Vary as a list of response fields the server changed during negotiation.
cards.explanation: Vary signals negotiated selection by naming request fields that influenced it. Different values for those fields might produce a different representation.
cards.misconception: Vary lists changed response fields rather than influential request fields.

cards.statement: `If-Match` lets an origin server match weak entity tags by comparing their quoted values.
cards.explanation: An origin server uses strong comparison for If-Match. Matching tags have to be strong and have identical opaque values.
cards.misconception: Matching quoted entity-tag values is sufficient for If-Match even when the tags are weak.

cards.statement: A client may use `If-None-Match: *` on PUT to protect an existing representation from replacement.
cards.explanation: If-None-Match: * fails when the target already has a current representation. It makes PUT conditional on the absence of a current representation.

cards.statement: An origin server returns 304 when it evaluates a failing `If-None-Match` condition on POST.
cards.explanation: An evaluated If-None-Match failure produces 412 for POST. The 304 response applies to GET and HEAD.
cards.misconception: A failed If-None-Match condition produces 304 regardless of the request method.

cards.statement: A server can give request preconditions priority over a 401 determined before processing content.
cards.explanation: A server ignores preconditions when the unconditional response, determined before processing content, is neither 2xx nor 412. An existing 401 takes precedence.
cards.misconception: Conditional request fields take precedence over an independently determined authentication error.

cards.statement: A server may answer a valid GET range request with 200 and the whole selected representation.
cards.explanation: A server may ignore the Range field. A valid range request therefore does not guarantee a partial response.

cards.statement: A client requesting `Range: bytes=20-40` includes byte 40 in the requested interval.
cards.explanation: Both endpoints of a byte range are inclusive. The requested interval includes its final byte position.

cards.statement: A client requesting `Range: bytes=-500` asks for bytes starting at offset 500.
cards.explanation: A suffix range asks for the final 500 bytes. If the representation is shorter, the range covers the entire representation.
cards.misconception: A byte range with an omitted starting position begins at the supplied offset.

cards.statement: A server returning several separate ranges in one 206 response uses `multipart/byteranges` content.
cards.explanation: A 206 response with several range parts uses multipart/byteranges. Each part carries a Content-Range field for its own interval.

cards.statement: A server's `Content-Range: bytes */8000` in a 416 response reports an 8000-byte representation.
cards.explanation: The number after */ in a 416 Content-Range reports the current length of the selected representation. A server should send this field for an unsatisfied byte range.

cards.statement: On a GET that would otherwise produce 200, a server answers a failed `If-Range` condition with 412.
cards.explanation: On a GET that otherwise yields 200, a failed If-Range makes the server ignore Range and send the whole representation, rather than 412.
cards.misconception: If-Range behaves like an ordinary failed precondition that produces 412.

cards.statement: A cache supporting several methods may key entries by target URI alone under HTTP's minimum key rule.
cards.explanation: HTTP's cache key includes at least the request method and target URI. In a cache dedicated to GET, the method is implicit.
cards.misconception: The target URI fully distinguishes cached responses across request methods.

source.title: RFC 9111, Section 2: Overview of Cache Operation

cards.statement: A shared cache may reuse a response to a request with Authorization if response Cache-Control includes public.
cards.explanation: The public response directive permits shared reuse despite Authorization, subject to the response's other caching restrictions.

source.title: RFC 9111, Section 3.5: Storing Responses to Authenticated Requests

cards.statement: A cache classifies a GET response with status 404 as heuristically cacheable.
cards.explanation: The 404 status is heuristically cacheable. Heuristics apply when explicit freshness is absent and other storage conditions permit caching.

cards.statement: A cache may treat `Vary: *` as matching any request's field values.
cards.explanation: A stored response with Vary: * always fails cache matching, even when the later request resembles the original one.
cards.misconception: Vary's asterisk matches arbitrary request field values like a glob.

source.title: RFC 9111, Section 4.1: Calculating Cache Keys with Vary

cards.statement: A cache treats a Vary-nominated field's absence in both requests as a match.
cards.explanation: A request field named by Vary matches in the absent-field case when it is absent from both the original and later request.

source.title: RFC 9111, Section 4.1: Calculating Cache Keys with Vary

cards.statement: A cache uses arrival order to select the newest of several equally suitable stored responses.
cards.explanation: A cache uses Date to determine the newest suitable stored response, rather than the order in which responses arrived.
cards.misconception: The newest response is the one that most recently reached the cache.

source.title: RFC 9111, Section 4: Constructing Responses from Caches

cards.statement: A cache may treat a 5xx received during validation as an absent server response.
cards.explanation: After a validation 5xx, a cache can follow the rules for a server that failed to respond, instead of forwarding that error.

source.title: RFC 9111, Section 4.3.3: Handling a Validation Response

cards.statement: A cache updating from a 304 keeps the old Cache-Control value when the 304 supplies a different one.
cards.explanation: When a 304 supplies updated Cache-Control, the cache replaces the corresponding field in each stored response identified for updating.
cards.misconception: A 304 leaves the stored response's Cache-Control unchanged.

source.title: RFC 9111, Section 4.3.4: Freshening Stored Responses upon Validation

cards.statement: A cache should update a stored GET response after a suitable 200 HEAD response with matching metadata.
cards.explanation: Matching received validators and any supplied Content-Length let the cache update the stored GET metadata.

source.title: RFC 9111, Section 4.3.5: Freshening Responses with HEAD

cards.statement: A range-capable cache may combine stored pieces for one target URI that share a strong validator.
cards.explanation: For a target URI, a common strong validator ensures that stored ranges identify the same representation version, allowing a cache to assemble them.

cards.statement: A cache that receives a successful PUT response waits for freshness to expire before invalidating the target.
cards.explanation: A cache must invalidate the target URI upon receiving a 2xx or 3xx response to an unsafe request, including PUT.
cards.misconception: A successful unsafe request affects cached responses when their freshness expires.

cards.statement: HTTP requires a cache to honor the Cache-Control directives in a client's request.
cards.explanation: Request directives are advisory: a cache may implement them, rather than being required to obey them.
cards.misconception: Request Cache-Control directives impose mandatory behavior on caches.

cards.statement: A client accepts stale responses of any age with a bare `Cache-Control: max-stale` request directive.
cards.explanation: The bare max-stale directive places no upper bound on acceptable staleness.

cards.statement: A cache treats request `no-store` as an instruction to delete its previously stored response.
cards.explanation: Request no-store does not affect a response already stored when the cache uses it to satisfy the request.
cards.misconception: Sending request no-store purges the existing stored response.

cards.statement: A cache honoring `only-if-cached` should return 504 when it lacks a suitable stored response.
cards.explanation: RFC 9111 recommends 504 Gateway Timeout when an honoring cache cannot supply a response meeting the request's constraints.

cards.statement: A disconnected cache must return an error for a stale response marked `must-revalidate`.
cards.explanation: Disconnection does not relax must-revalidate: a cache must report an error rather than reuse the stale response.

cards.statement: A cache restricts heuristic freshness for `public` responses to HTTP's usual heuristically cacheable status codes.
cards.explanation: A public response with no explicit freshness information is heuristically cacheable, including when its status code normally lacks that property.
cards.misconception: Public leaves eligibility for heuristic freshness confined to the usual status-code list.

cards.statement: A cache that implements `must-understand` and the status code's caching rules should ignore an accompanying `no-store`.
cards.explanation: RFC 9111 has senders pair must-understand with no-store, so caches lacking that support store nothing, while a cache meeting both conditions should ignore no-store.

cards.statement: Under RFC 8246, a client honoring `immutable` skips revalidation once the stored response is stale.
cards.explanation: RFC 8246 limits immutable to the stored response's freshness lifetime: once that response is stale, a client should revalidate it as it would without immutable.
cards.misconception: immutable means a stored response never needs revalidation, even after it goes stale.

cards.statement: A cache targeting `CDN-Cache-Control` may combine its valid policy with `Cache-Control` in the same response.
cards.explanation: A cache using a valid targeted field chooses its policy and ignores Cache-Control and Expires for that response.
cards.misconception: A targeted cache combines targeted and general policies instead of selecting the targeted policy.

cards.statement: An origin server should keep several Set-Cookie fields separate in an HTTP response.
cards.explanation: Combining Set-Cookie fields with commas can change their meaning because cookie syntax already uses commas.

cards.statement: A user agent separates cookie name-value pairs with semicolons in the Cookie request field.
cards.explanation: The Cookie field separates successive cookie pairs with a semicolon and a space.

cards.statement: A user agent includes a cookie's Path attribute alongside its value in the Cookie request field.
cards.explanation: The Cookie request field omits the attributes supplied with Set-Cookie. The server does not receive the cookie's Path attribute in that field.
cards.misconception: Cookie requests return stored cookie attributes alongside their values.

cards.statement: A user agent replaces a stored cookie after accepting another with the same name, domain and path.
cards.explanation: The name, domain and path identify the stored cookie. An accepted cookie with the same combination takes its place.

cards.statement: A user agent gives a cookie subdomain scope by default when the server omits Domain.
cards.explanation: Omitting Domain creates a host-only cookie. Its host must exactly match the request host for the cookie to be selected.
cards.misconception: Omitting Domain extends a cookie's host scope to subdomains.

source.title: RFC 6265, Sections 5.3 and 5.4: Storage and Sending

cards.statement: A user agent may accept `Domain=example.com` on a cookie set by `shop.example.com`.
cards.explanation: The host shop.example.com domain-matches example.com. A server can therefore set a cookie with that parent domain.

cards.statement: A user agent defaults a cookie's Path to `/guide/page.html` for a request to `/guide/page.html`.
cards.explanation: For /guide/page.html, RFC 6265's default-path algorithm yields /guide by removing the final slash and the portion after it.
cards.misconception: A cookie's default path includes the request path's final file component.

cards.statement: A server deletes a stored cookie by setting its value to an empty string.
cards.explanation: An empty cookie value can remain stored. To request deletion, the server sends a matching cookie with an expiry in the past.
cards.misconception: An empty cookie value acts as a deletion instruction.

cards.statement: A user agent may evict a stored cookie before its specified expiry time because of memory pressure.
cards.explanation: Expiry sets a maximum lifetime, not guaranteed retention. A user agent may remove cookies earlier because of resource limits or user preferences.

cards.statement: RFC 6265 uses the setting server's port as a matching condition when a user agent selects outgoing cookies.
cards.explanation: Cookies are shared across ports on a host. Cookie scope does not include the port on which the server set the cookie.
cards.misconception: Cookie delivery matches the port that originally set the cookie.

cards.statement: A cookie-enabled user agent processes Set-Cookie fields in HTTP error responses.
cards.explanation: An HTTP error status does not itself suppress Set-Cookie processing. Cookie-enabled user agents process these fields subject to cookie acceptance policies.

cards.statement: With fetch(), a browser lets scripts read Set-Cookie through response.headers on a same-origin response.
cards.explanation: The Fetch Standard filters Set-Cookie from response headers exposed to scripts, including on same-origin responses.
cards.misconception: Scripts can read a same-origin network response's Set-Cookie field through fetch().

cards.statement: An HTTP/1.1 client may use just the path and query as the target of a GET sent to a forward proxy.
cards.explanation: For a GET sent to a forward proxy, HTTP/1.1 requires an absolute-form target, including the URI's scheme and authority.
cards.misconception: A forward-proxy request uses the same path-only target as a direct origin request.

cards.statement: A server answers an HTTP/1.1 request that omits the Host field with 400 Bad Request.
cards.explanation: RFC 9112 makes a server send 400 for any HTTP/1.1 request that lacks Host, and for any request with more than one Host field line or an invalid Host value.

cards.statement: An HTTP/1.1 recipient treats a connection as persistent by default.
cards.explanation: The HTTP/1.1 persistence default lets later requests reuse the connection after the current response.

cards.statement: An HTTP/1.0 client requests persistence by sending a Keep-Alive field alone.
cards.explanation: HTTP/1.0 persistence is negotiated with the keep-alive option in Connection. A Keep-Alive field alone does not request it.
cards.misconception: The Keep-Alive field itself activates persistence in HTTP/1.0.

cards.statement: An HTTP/1.1 recipient can detect the end of chunked content while keeping the connection open.
cards.explanation: Chunked framing signals message completion independently of a closed connection, so a recipient can retain the connection.

cards.statement: An HTTP/1.1 client may delimit its request content by closing the connection.
cards.explanation: HTTP/1.1 request content needs explicit framing by length or transfer coding; connection closure does not delimit it.
cards.misconception: Connection closure serves as a valid framing delimiter for HTTP/1.1 request content.

cards.statement: An HTTP/1.1 recipient uses Content-Length ahead of Transfer-Encoding when both fields occur.
cards.explanation: Transfer-Encoding overrides Content-Length. RFC 9112 says a message carrying both fields ought to be handled as an error.
cards.misconception: Content-Length takes priority over Transfer-Encoding when both occur.

cards.statement: An HTTP/1.1 server may answer a chunked request with 411 when it requires Content-Length.
cards.explanation: A server may reject request content that lacks Content-Length with 411, including content framed with chunked transfer coding.

cards.statement: An HTTP/1.1 server returns pipelined responses in the order their processing finishes.
cards.explanation: A server sends responses to pipelined HTTP/1.1 requests in request order, even if it processes safe requests in parallel.
cards.misconception: Pipelined HTTP/1.1 responses can be returned in completion order.

cards.statement: An HTTP/1.1 proxy removes fields named by Connection before forwarding an HTTP message.
cards.explanation: A forwarding proxy removes fields nominated by Connection because those fields apply to the incoming connection.

cards.statement: An HTTP/1.1 server names the selected protocol in Upgrade when it sends 101 Switching Protocols.
cards.explanation: A 101 response must include Upgrade to identify the protocol selected for the existing connection.

cards.statement: An HTTP/1.1 client may use Upgrade to move the conversation from TCP to UDP.
cards.explanation: Upgrade changes the protocol running over the existing connection. It does not replace the connection's transport protocol.
cards.misconception: Upgrade replaces the underlying transport along with the application protocol.

cards.statement: In HTTP/2, a client can interleave several request streams over a single TCP connection.
cards.explanation: Separate HTTP exchanges use separate streams whose frames share one connection, allowing requests to overlap.

cards.statement: In HTTP/2, an endpoint may charge a HEADERS frame against its advertised stream flow-control window.
cards.explanation: HTTP/2 flow control governs DATA frames. HEADERS frames do not consume the advertised flow-control window.
cards.misconception: HTTP/2 flow control applies to header transmission as well as content transmission.

cards.statement: In HTTP/2, a recipient treats an uppercase letter in a field name as making the message malformed.
cards.explanation: HTTP/2 senders lowercase field names, and recipients treat an uppercase field name as a malformed message.

cards.statement: In HTTP/2, a sender places pseudo-header fields after the regular fields in a header section.
cards.explanation: A sender puts pseudo-header fields before regular fields. A pseudo-header appearing after a regular field makes the message malformed.
cards.misconception: HTTP/2 pseudo-header fields follow ordinary fields.

cards.statement: An HTTP/2 proxy can send `Connection: close` to end persistence after its response.
cards.explanation: HTTP/2 prohibits the Connection field. An HTTP/2 message containing it is malformed.
cards.misconception: HTTP/1.1's Connection field remains usable for HTTP/2 connection management.

cards.statement: In HTTP/2, a client must make an included Host identify the same authority as `:authority`.
cards.explanation: A client must not send Host identifying a different authority from :authority. Their values are normalized for comparison.

cards.statement: An HTTP/2 server treats a POST whose content-length differs from its DATA content size as malformed.
cards.explanation: For a message carrying content, content-length has to match the total content conveyed in DATA frames.

cards.statement: An HTTP/2 client selects `h2` through the Upgrade field when establishing an HTTPS connection.
cards.explanation: HTTP/2 over TLS selects h2 through the TLS ALPN extension during connection establishment.
cards.misconception: HTTP/2 over HTTPS uses HTTP Upgrade for protocol selection.

cards.statement: An HTTP/2 client may reuse an HTTPS connection across origins when the server has authority for both.
cards.explanation: Connection reuse across HTTPS origins depends on server authority, including a certificate valid for the new origin's host.

cards.statement: An HTTP/2 proxy chosen by the client may generate 421 for an origin it lacks authority to serve.
cards.explanation: A proxy must not generate 421. An origin server or its gateway uses 421 to reject a target URI outside its authority or connection context.
cards.misconception: A proxy can generate 421 to reject a request for an origin it cannot authoritatively serve.

cards.statement: An HTTP/3 client carries QUIC traffic over TCP when it connects to an origin server.
cards.explanation: HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP. Its reliable transport comes from QUIC rather than a TCP connection.
cards.misconception: HTTP/3 keeps TCP as the transport beneath QUIC.

cards.statement: An HTTP/3 receiver can make progress on another stream while packet loss blocks one request stream.
cards.explanation: QUIC supplies reliability per stream, so loss affecting one stream does not impose a connection-wide delivery stall.

cards.statement: An HTTP/3 client may directly access an `http` URI's authoritative server over QUIC.
cards.explanation: HTTP/3 cannot directly access an http URI's authoritative server. Such access needs another mechanism to identify an authoritative HTTP/3 service.
cards.misconception: HTTP/3 can use the usual http URI authority directly over QUIC.

cards.statement: An HTTP/3 client can use connection IDs to retain its QUIC connection when its network address changes.
cards.explanation: Connection IDs let QUIC associate packets with an existing connection despite changes to the client's address or network path.

cards.statement: A server may answer an early-data request with 425 when processing it risks replay.
cards.explanation: A 425 Too Early response signals that the server declines the risk of processing a request that might be replayed.

source.title: RFC 8470, Section 5.2: The 425 (Too Early) Status Code

cards.statement: A user agent groups `http://example.com:443` and `https://example.com:443` into the same origin.
cards.explanation: The http and https schemes identify distinct origins with separate namespaces, even when the host names match.
cards.misconception: Matching host names make http and https URLs part of one origin.

cards.statement: A client using Alt-Svc switches the resource's origin to the alternative service's host.
cards.explanation: Alt-Svc changes the connection route while the URI's original scheme, host and port continue to identify the resource's origin.
cards.misconception: Using an alternative service moves the resource to a new origin at the alternative's host.

cards.statement: A client can authenticate an Alt-Svc endpoint on another host using a certificate valid for that host alone.
cards.explanation: An Alt-Svc alternative must prove authority for the origin's host. A certificate covering just its different network host is insufficient.
cards.misconception: An alternative service's certificate needs to cover its own host rather than the origin's host.

cards.statement: A client treats an Alt-Svc advertisement as fresh for 24 hours by default from message generation.
cards.explanation: Alt-Svc advertisements have a 24-hour freshness lifetime unless the ma parameter supplies a different lifetime.

source.title: RFC 7838 §3.1: Caching Alt-Svc Header Field Values

cards.statement: A client treats `persist=1` as extending an Alt-Svc entry beyond its advertised freshness lifetime.
cards.explanation: The persist=1 parameter signals usefulness across network changes. It does not extend the entry's freshness lifetime.
cards.misconception: The persist parameter keeps an Alt-Svc entry usable after its freshness expires.

source.title: RFC 7838 §3.1: Caching Alt-Svc Header Field Values

cards.statement: With fetch(), a browser uses cors mode by default when its input is a URL string.
cards.explanation: A URL-string input makes fetch() construct a request in cors mode unless the caller supplies another mode.

cards.statement: With fetch(), a browser gives a cross-origin HTTP response type basic when the request uses no-cors mode.
cards.explanation: A cross-origin HTTP response to a no-cors request has type opaque. Scripts cannot read its response headers or content.
cards.misconception: The no-cors mode returns a basic response that scripts can inspect.

cards.statement: With fetch(), a browser adds the Origin header to a same-origin HTTP POST request.
cards.explanation: The Origin header accompanies methods other than GET and HEAD, including when the request stays on the page's origin.

cards.statement: A browser treats `Range: bytes=-500` as a CORS-safelisted request header.
cards.explanation: The CORS safelist requires an explicit starting offset. A suffix range such as bytes=-500 falls outside it.
cards.misconception: The CORS safelist accepts a suffix byte range as a single-range value.

cards.statement: In the Fetch Standard, a cross-origin fetch() POST with a ReadableStream body goes through CORS preflight.
cards.explanation: A ReadableStream request body sets the request's use-CORS-preflight flag, so a cross-origin request is preflighted even with a safelisted method and headers.

cards.statement: With fetch(), a browser sends cookies on a cross-origin preflight for credentials mode include.
cards.explanation: A CORS preflight excludes credentials even when the subsequent request uses credentials mode include.
cards.misconception: A preflight inherits the actual request's credential inclusion.

source.title: MDN: CORS preflight requests and credentials

cards.statement: A browser accepts a 403 preflight response when its CORS permission headers authorize the request.
cards.explanation: A successful CORS preflight needs an ok status. Permission headers do not make a 403 successful.
cards.misconception: Permission headers make an HTTP error status acceptable for a preflight.

cards.statement: A browser can use a preflight response's Allow field to authorize the requested CORS method.
cards.explanation: Allow is irrelevant to CORS permission. Access-Control-Allow-Methods provides the preflight's method permission.
cards.misconception: Allow supplies method permission for a CORS preflight.

cards.statement: A browser may cache preflight permissions for five seconds when the server omits Access-Control-Max-Age.
cards.explanation: The default preflight-cache lifetime is five seconds. Access-Control-Max-Age supplies a different lifetime when present.

cards.statement: In the Fetch Standard, `Access-Control-Allow-Headers: *` covers the Authorization request header.
cards.explanation: The Fetch Standard makes Authorization a CORS non-wildcard request-header name, so a preflight passes only when Access-Control-Allow-Headers names it explicitly.
cards.misconception: A * in Access-Control-Allow-Headers covers every request header, Authorization included.

source.title: Fetch Standard: CORS non-wildcard request-header name

cards.statement: A browser compares the true value in Access-Control-Allow-Credentials using case-sensitive matching.
cards.explanation: The valid permission value is lowercase true. Other capitalization fails the credentials-value comparison.

cards.statement: fetch() rejects its promise when a same-origin server responds with 500 Internal Server Error.
cards.explanation: An HTTP 500 response fulfills fetch() with a Response object. An HTTP error status alone does not cause rejection.
cards.misconception: An HTTP error status makes fetch() reject its promise.

cards.statement: A Response object reports `ok: true` for an exposed status from 200 through 299.
cards.explanation: The ok getter classifies the exposed status as successful; it does not inspect the response content.

cards.statement: With `redirect: "manual"`, fetch() lets scripts read Location from a same-origin redirect response.
cards.explanation: A redirect received in manual mode produces an opaqueredirect Response with an empty exposed header list.
cards.misconception: Manual redirect handling exposes the redirect's Location field to scripts.

cards.statement: fetch() uses the `same-origin` credentials mode by default when a script passes a URL string.
cards.explanation: The default credentials policy includes credentials for same-origin requests. A script can change the policy through the credentials option.

cards.statement: fetch() requires `mode: "cors"` when a script uses the `only-if-cached` cache option.
cards.explanation: The only-if-cached cache mode requires same-origin request mode. Pairing it with cors is invalid.
cards.misconception: The only-if-cached cache mode works with cors request mode.

cards.statement: For fetch() with `cache: "default"` and If-Match, the user agent handles the HTTP cache as `no-store`.
cards.explanation: A script-supplied If-Match makes the internal HTTP request use no-store when its cache mode starts as default.

cards.statement: The Request constructor accepts a GET body when the origin server has indicated support.
cards.explanation: The Request constructor throws a TypeError for a GET request with a body, regardless of the origin server's support.
cards.misconception: Server support lets the Request constructor accept GET request content.

cards.statement: The Request constructor throws a TypeError for a URL containing a nonempty username or password.
cards.explanation: The constructor rejects credentials embedded in the URL instead of using them to authenticate the request.

cards.statement: The Request constructor requires `duplex: "half"` when a script supplies a ReadableStream body.
cards.explanation: A ReadableStream supplied as the request body needs an explicit duplex option, whose defined value is half.

cards.statement: A script calling Headers.get() receives an array when a field has several appended values.
cards.explanation: Headers.get() returns one string, joining repeated values in insertion order with a comma and a space.
cards.misconception: Headers.get() returns repeated field values as separate array entries.

cards.statement: fetch() automatically converts the method string `patch` to `PATCH` when constructing a request.
cards.explanation: Fetch's method normalization leaves patch as written. A script needs to supply PATCH to request the standard method.
cards.misconception: Fetch uppercases patch as it does certain other standard methods.
